en.title: Petroleum Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What petroleum engineering covers, how degrees are organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What petroleum engineering is
sections.text:
Petroleum engineering is the branch of engineering that finds, extracts and prepares oil and gas for use. It applies mathematics, physics, chemistry, geology and economics to hidden underground reservoirs and to surface operations. It includes drilling wells, designing completions, estimating reserves, predicting flow, lifting fluids, processing oil and gas, and judging safety, environmental impact and cost. It works closely with geology and geophysics but does not replace them.

The work is uncertain because reservoirs are remote and data are sparse. Models are approximations, not truth. These summaries teach principles. They do not replace standards, regulations, company procedures or a registered engineer. Codes and regulators differ by country. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering practice. API and ISO standards are widely used in industry, but national law and company rules also apply. Check the current official source.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BEng in petroleum engineering commonly takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. In the UK, a BEng commonly takes three years and an MEng four; in Scotland each usually takes a year longer. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree commonly takes four years. A master’s degree usually adds one to two years.

The early years are shared with other engineering students: mathematics, chemistry, physics, fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, geology and computing. Later years add reservoir, drilling, production, facilities, economics, safety and a design project. Professional registration is separate from the degree. In Nigeria, graduates can pursue COREN registration after the required experience and examinations. Other countries have their own bodies and rules. Do not assume that one country’s route applies everywhere.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
First come the foundation subjects: engineering mathematics, chemistry of hydrocarbons, physics and mechanics, fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, petroleum geology and earth science, introduction to the profession, and engineering computing and numerical methods. These give the language and tools for later work.

The core follows. Reservoir rock properties and reservoir fluid properties and phase behaviour describe what is in the ground. Drilling systems and operations, well design, cementing and well control explain how to reach it. Formation evaluation and well logging measure it. Well completion and stimulation connect the well to the reservoir. Reservoir engineering fundamentals and reservoir performance prediction and decline analysis estimate how much can be recovered. Production engineering and nodal analysis, artificial lift, surface facilities and pipeline transport, and natural gas engineering deal with bringing fluids to market. Refining basics, enhanced oil recovery, petroleum economics and reserves, health, safety and environment, professional practice and ethics, and research methods and design project complete the core.

At master’s level come advanced reservoir simulation, petroleum geomechanics, unconventional resources and advanced hydraulic fracturing, and research methods and dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study with a pen and paper. Draw the reservoir, the well or the process before you write equations. Write units on every line and convert them before calculating. Learn typical ranges for porosity, permeability, pressure and flow rate so that you can notice an unreasonable answer.

Practise hand calculations before using software. Then use software and check it against a simple case. Read the assumptions in every correlation and do not use it outside its range. Keep a formula sheet with the meaning of each symbol. Work past questions and explain your steps to a classmate. Take laboratory, field and industrial training seriously. Learn the safety rules and the reasons behind them. Read the current regulations and standards for the country where you plan to work.

keyPoints: Petroleum engineering finds, extracts and prepares oil and gas, using geology, physics, chemistry, mathematics and economics.
Degree length, awards and registration rules differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and regulator.

Understand hand methods and assumptions before trusting software or correlations.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for petroleum engineering
en.short: Calculus, linear algebra, ODEs and numerical methods for petroleum problems, with units and dimensional checks.

sections.heading: Units and calculus
sections.text: Petroleum quantities carry units. A valid equation is dimensionally homogeneous: both sides have the same dimensions. Convert to consistent SI before calculating; for example 1 bar = 100 kPa and 1 psi ≈ 6.895 kPa. Calculus describes change: the derivative dy/dx is a rate, and the integral accumulates a quantity. Example: pressure gradient dp/dz = ρg. With ρ = 850 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s², dp/dz = 850 × 9.81 = 8,338.5 Pa/m ≈ 8.34 kPa/m. The units check: kg/m³ × m/s² = kg/(m² s²) = Pa/m.

sections.heading: Linear algebra
sections.text: Linear algebra solves coupled balances. Write a system as Ax = b, where A holds coefficients, x the unknowns and b the known values. Gaussian elimination reduces A to triangular form; the determinant shows whether a unique solution exists. Example: 2x + y = 10 and x + 3y = 15. The determinant is 2×3 − 1×1 = 5. Then x = (10×3 − 1×15) ÷ 5 = 15 ÷ 5 = 3, and y = (2×15 − 10×1) ÷ 5 = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Check: 2×3 + 4 = 10 and 3 + 3×4 = 15.

sections.heading: ODEs and numerics
sections.text: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates a function to its derivatives. The separable ODE dP/dt = −kP has solution P = P0 e^(−kt), a simple decline model. Numerical methods approximate answers when no closed form is available. Euler’s method uses y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(t(n), y(n)). Newton-Raphson finds roots with x(n+1) = x(n) − f(x(n)) ÷ f′(x(n)). Numerical integration, such as the trapezoidal rule, approximates an integral by summing areas. Example: solve f(x) = x² − 2 from x0 = 1. x1 = 1 − (1 − 2) ÷ 2 = 1.5; x2 = 1.5 − (2.25 − 2) ÷ 3 = 1.4167, approaching √2 = 1.4142. Always check units and substitute back.

keyPoints: Check dimensional homogeneity and convert all inputs to consistent SI units before calculating.
The derivative gives a rate of change and the integral accumulates: dp/dz = ρg and P = P0 e^(−kt) for dP/dt = −kP.
Solve Ax = b by Gaussian elimination; a nonzero determinant means a unique solution.
Euler’s method: y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(t(n), y(n)).
Newton-Raphson: x(n+1) = x(n) − f(x(n)) ÷ f′(x(n)).
Substitute answers back and check units; numerical results need convergence and error checks.

en.title: Chemistry of hydrocarbons and petroleum fluids
en.short: Atomic bonding, moles, hydrocarbon families and refining chemistry for petroleum fluids.

sections.heading: Atoms and bonds
sections.text: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells. The outer electrons, or valence electrons, control bonding. Carbon has four valence electrons, so it forms four covalent bonds: shared electron pairs. Petroleum bonds are mostly covalent and nearly nonpolar between carbon and hydrogen. Molecules are held by weak van der Waals forces, so boiling points rise with molecular size and less branching. Ionic and metallic bonding matter in minerals and metals, not hydrocarbons.

sections.heading: Moles and stoichiometry
sections.text: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles; molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams. A balanced equation gives mole ratios. For methane: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Molar masses: CH4 = 16 g/mol, O2 = 32, CO2 = 44, H2O = 18. Burning 16 g methane needs 64 g oxygen and gives 44 g carbon dioxide and 36 g water. Mass balance: 16 + 64 = 80 = 44 + 36.

sections.heading: Hydrocarbon families
sections.text: Alkanes have only single carbon-carbon bonds and are saturated: general formula CnH2n+2. Methane and octane are examples. Cycloalkanes (naphthenes) are saturated carbon rings. Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond, CnH2n for one double bond, and are unsaturated and more reactive. Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring, a planar six-carbon ring with delocalised electrons. Crude oil is mainly alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatics; alkenes are minor in crude but common in cracked products. Functional groups are atom groups that set reactivity: sulfur as thiols (-SH) and sulfides (-S-), nitrogen mostly in ring compounds, and oxygen as carboxylic acids (-COOH), concentrated in heavier fractions. Sulfur and nitrogen compounds poison catalysts and pollute.

sections.heading: Refining chemistry
sections.text: Refining uses chemistry to separate and change molecules. Distillation separates by boiling point, which depends on size and branching. Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes. Reforming rearranges alkanes into aromatics and branched molecules to raise octane number. Hydrotreating adds hydrogen to remove sulfur and nitrogen as H2S and NH3. Alkylation joins small alkenes with isobutane to make high-octane branched alkanes. Processes and limits vary by refinery and country.

keyPoints: Carbon forms four covalent bonds; alkanes are saturated CnH2n+2, alkenes have C=C and aromatics have a benzene ring.
A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles and molar mass is grams per mole.
Balanced equations give mole ratios; methane burns as CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, and 16 g CH4 needs 64 g O2.
Boiling point rises with molecular size and falls with branching because van der Waals forces are weaker.
Cracking makes alkenes, reforming makes aromatics, and hydrotreating removes sulfur and nitrogen.
Petroleum contains minor sulfur, nitrogen and oxygen functional groups that affect refining and pollution.

en.title: Physics and mechanics for petroleum engineering
en.short: Forces, energy, pressure, elasticity, waves and heat for rock, fluid and drilling calculations.

sections.heading: Force and motion
sections.text: Newtonian mechanics treats force as the cause of change in motion. Newton’s second law is F = ma, where F is net force in newtons, m is mass in kilograms and a is acceleration in m/s². Weight is W = mg, with g about 9.81 m/s² near the Earth’s surface. Momentum p = mv is conserved when no external force acts. These ideas explain loads on drill strings and falling objects.

sections.heading: Work, energy and pressure
sections.text: Work is W = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Kinetic energy is 1/2 mv² and gravitational potential energy is mgh. Energy is conserved when friction is neglected. Pressure is p = F ÷ A, force per unit area. In a static fluid, gauge pressure (pressure measured relative to atmospheric) rises with depth: p = ρgh, where ρ is density and h is depth. Example: at 2,000 m depth in water of density 1,000 kg/m³, p = 1,000 × 9.81 × 2,000 = 19.62 MPa. On 0.01 m², F = pA = 196,200 N.

sections.heading: Elasticity and waves
sections.text: Stress is force per area and strain is fractional deformation. For small elastic strain, Hooke’s law gives stress = E × strain, where E is Young’s modulus. A rod of length L and area A stretches by ΔL = FL ÷ (AE). Waves have speed v = fλ, where f is frequency and λ is wavelength. Seismic and acoustic methods use this relation to link travel time and distance.

sections.heading: Heat and expansion
sections.text: Heat is energy transferred because of temperature difference. The sensible heat to change temperature is Q = mcΔT, where c is specific heat capacity. Thermal expansion is ΔL = αLΔT, with α the linear expansion coefficient. Heat conduction rate through a solid is kAΔT ÷ L, where k is thermal conductivity. These ideas matter when drilling fluids, casing and rock change temperature. Check material properties in current tables; values vary with temperature and composition.

keyPoints: Newton’s second law is F = ma; weight is mg.
Work is Fd cos θ; kinetic energy is 1/2 mv² and potential energy is mgh.
Pressure is F ÷ A, and static fluid pressure rises as p = ρgh.
Hooke’s law gives stress = E × strain, and extension ΔL = FL ÷ (AE).
Wave speed is v = fλ; sensible heat is Q = mcΔT.
Thermal expansion is ΔL = αLΔT; check material data because properties vary.

en.title: Fluid mechanics foundations
en.short: Fluid properties, hydrostatics, pressure, continuity, Bernoulli, flow regime and pipe friction.

sections.heading: Properties and pressure
sections.text:
A fluid deforms continuously under shear stress. Density ρ is mass per volume; specific weight is ρg. Dynamic viscosity μ measures resistance to shear and has units Pa·s; kinematic viscosity ν = μ ÷ ρ has units m²/s. Liquids usually become less viscous when heated, gases more viscous.

In a static fluid, pressure at depth h is p = p0 + ρgh, where p0 is surface pressure. Pressure acts equally in all directions at a point. A manometer measures pressure difference as Δp = ρgΔh. Absolute pressure is measured from vacuum; gauge pressure from local atmosphere. Convert bar, psi and kPa carefully.

sections.heading: Flow and energy
sections.text:
For steady incompressible flow in a full pipe, continuity gives A1V1 = A2V2, where A is area and V is mean velocity.

The Bernoulli equation along a streamline without losses is p ÷ (ρg) + V² ÷ (2g) + z = constant. The terms are pressure head, velocity head and elevation head in metres. With friction or a pump, add head loss or pump head. Bernoulli is energy conservation for steady, frictionless, incompressible flow.

sections.heading: Friction and regime
sections.text:
Pipe flow is laminar when fluid moves in smooth layers and turbulent when eddies mix it. The Reynolds number Re = ρVD ÷ μ = VD ÷ ν indicates the regime. In a circular pipe, transition is roughly Re = 2000 to 4000, but it varies.

For laminar pipe flow, the Darcy friction factor is f = 64 ÷ Re. For turbulent flow, f depends on Re and relative roughness, the roughness height divided by pipe diameter. Darcy-Weisbach head loss is hf = fLV² ÷ (2gD).

Example: water, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, D = 0.10 m, V = 1.2 m/s, L = 50 m, f = 0.025.
hf = 0.025 × 50 × 1.2² ÷ (2 × 9.81 × 0.10) = 0.917 m
Pressure drop = ρghf = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.917 = 8,996 Pa, about 9.0 kPa.
Re = 1000 × 1.2 × 0.10 ÷ 0.001 = 120,000, so flow is turbulent.

keyPoints: Pressure in a static fluid: p = p0 + ρgh.
Continuity for incompressible pipe flow: A1V1 = A2V2.
Bernoulli without losses: p ÷ (ρg) + V² ÷ (2g) + z = constant.
Reynolds number: Re = ρVD ÷ μ; low Re is laminar, high Re is turbulent.
Darcy-Weisbach head loss: hf = fLV² ÷ (2gD); for laminar flow f = 64 ÷ Re.
Check units and convert pressure and viscosity to consistent SI units before calculating.

en.title: Thermodynamics foundations for petroleum systems
en.short: First and second laws, properties, ideal and real gas behaviour, phase equilibrium and energy balances.

sections.heading: Laws and properties
sections.text:
Thermodynamics deals with energy, heat and work. A system is what we study; the surroundings are the rest. Properties are intensive (temperature, pressure) or extensive (mass, volume, total energy). State functions depend only on the present state: internal energy U, enthalpy H = U + PV, entropy S.

First law: ΔU = Q − W for a closed system, where Q is heat added and W is work done by the system. Second law: entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease; heat flows from hot to cold.

sections.heading: Gas behaviour
sections.text:
An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT, with absolute pressure P, volume V, amount n, absolute temperature T and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature. The compressibility factor z = PV/(nRT) measures this; z = 1 for ideal, so PV = znRT.

Example: 1 kmol of methane at 300 K and 5 MPa, ideal:
V = nRT ÷ P = 1000 × 8.314 × 300 ÷ (5 × 10⁶) = 0.499 m³.

sections.heading: Phase equilibrium
sections.text: A phase is a distinct physical form, such as liquid or gas. At equilibrium, temperature and pressure are uniform and the chemical potential of each component is the same in every phase; equivalently, the fugacity (a pressure-like measure of escaping tendency) is the same. For a pure substance, liquid and vapour coexist at the saturation pressure, which depends on temperature. For mixtures, equilibrium ratios K describe how each component splits between gas and liquid.

sections.heading: Energy balances
sections.text:
An energy balance applies the first law. For steady flow with negligible kinetic and potential changes, Q − W = ΔH, where W is work done by the system. A throttling valve has Q ≈ 0 and W = 0, so ΔH ≈ 0 (isenthalpic). A compressor requires work input, so W is negative.

Example: a cooler removes 20 kJ with no work, so ΔH = Q = −20 kJ; enthalpy falls by 20 kJ.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: ΔU = Q − W.
Second law: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
Enthalpy is H = U + PV; entropy S measures energy dispersal.
Ideal gas law: PV = nRT; real gas: PV = znRT.
At phase equilibrium, fugacity is equal in all phases.
Steady-flow energy balance: Q − W = ΔH when kinetic and potential changes are negligible.

en.title: Petroleum geology and earth science
en.short: Earth structure, rocks, source rock, maturation, migration, reservoirs, seals and traps.

sections.heading: Earth structure and rocks
sections.text:
The Earth has a crust, mantle and core. The rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that move, so basins form and sediments accumulate.

Rocks are igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic. Petroleum occurs almost entirely in sedimentary rocks because they form from deposited material and can preserve organic matter. Igneous and metamorphic rocks can hold oil only where fracturing or weathering has opened space for oil to migrate into.

sections.heading: Sediments and source rock
sections.text:
Weathering breaks rock, erosion removes it, transport carries grains, and deposition lays them down. Burial compacts the sediment and cementation hardens it into sedimentary rock.

A source rock is an organic-rich, fine-grained rock, usually shale or mudstone, deposited in quiet water where organic matter is preserved. Its organic matter becomes kerogen, the solid precursor of oil and gas.

sections.heading: Maturation and migration
sections.text:
As burial deepens, heat and time mature kerogen. At moderate temperatures it generates oil; at higher temperatures it generates gas. The exact temperature ranges vary by basin, so geologists use basin-specific models.

Migration is movement of hydrocarbons from the source rock towards a trap. Primary migration expels them from the source rock; secondary migration carries them along permeable beds or faults by buoyancy until a trap stops them.

sections.heading: Reservoir, seal and trap
sections.text:
A reservoir is porous and permeable rock, such as sandstone or limestone, that stores hydrocarbons. A seal, or cap rock, is impermeable, commonly shale or evaporite such as salt, and prevents escape. A trap is a geometry that holds buoyant hydrocarbons that migrate into it, such as an anticline, a fault block or a stratigraphic pinch-out, where a layer thins out.

A working petroleum system needs source, reservoir, seal, trap, migration and correct timing. In the Niger Delta, Nigeria, marine shales source oil, deltaic sands store it, shales seal it, and growth-fault rollover anticlines trap it.

keyPoints: Petroleum forms and accumulates mainly in sedimentary basins.
A source rock is organic-rich fine-grained rock whose kerogen matures with heat and time into oil and gas.
Migration moves hydrocarbons from source rock into reservoir rock, driven mainly by buoyancy.
A reservoir stores hydrocarbons, a seal prevents escape, and a trap concentrates them.
A working petroleum system needs source, reservoir, seal, trap, migration and correct timing.
In the Niger Delta, Nigeria, marine shales, deltaic sands, shales and growth-fault anticlines form a classic system.

en.title: Introduction to the petroleum engineering profession
en.short: The oil and gas value chain, exploration and production, reserves terms, units and engineering roles.

sections.heading: The value chain
sections.text: Petroleum engineering sits inside a value chain. Upstream covers exploration and production: finding oil and gas and bringing them to the surface. Midstream covers transport, storage and processing, including pipelines, tankers and gas plants. Downstream covers refining, distribution, retail and petrochemicals. The boundaries vary by company and country, but the chain helps you see where a job fits. A petroleum engineer may work upstream, midstream or downstream, and often with geologists, chemists, mechanical engineers and economists.

sections.heading: Exploration to production
sections.text: Exploration begins with geology and geophysics, including seismic surveys, to identify possible accumulations. An exploration well tests the idea. If a discovery is made, appraisal wells estimate its size and behaviour. Development then drills production wells and builds facilities. Production lifts fluids, separates oil, gas and water, and maintains flow. Eventually comes abandonment and restoration. The phrase exploration and production, or E and P, is often used for upstream.

sections.heading: Reserves and resources
sections.text: Resources are estimated quantities of petroleum in the ground. Reserves are the part judged commercially recoverable from known accumulations under stated conditions. Contingent resources are discovered but not yet commercial. Prospective resources are undiscovered. Reserves are therefore a subset of resources, and the estimate changes with price, technology, law and data. Always state the classification system and date. Do not treat a resource estimate as a reserve without evidence of commercial recovery.

sections.heading: Units and roles
sections.text: Common units are the barrel (bbl) for oil volume and the standard cubic foot (scf) or cubic metre for gas volume at stated standard conditions. One cubic metre equals about 6.2898 barrels, so 10,000 m³ is about 62,898 bbl. STOIIP means stock tank oil initially in place; GIIP means gas initially in place. Petroleum engineers work as reservoir, drilling, production or facilities engineers, and in health, safety and economics roles. Registration differs by country; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration, while other countries have their own bodies.

keyPoints: Upstream finds and produces, midstream moves and processes, downstream refines and sells.
Exploration, appraisal, development, production and abandonment are stages of upstream work.
Reserves are commercially recoverable resources; contingent and prospective resources are not reserves.
One cubic metre is about 6.2898 barrels; state standard conditions for gas volumes.
STOIIP and GIIP are initial in-place volumes, not reserves.
Petroleum engineers work across reservoir, drilling, production, facilities, safety and economics; registration is country-specific, for example COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Engineering computing and numerical methods
en.short: Programming basics, spreadsheets, root finding, interpolation, curve fitting and numerical integration.

sections.heading: Programming and spreadsheets
sections.text: An algorithm is a finite list of steps. In a program, variables store numbers, loops repeat steps and functions group reusable steps. Python is common because it is free and readable. A spreadsheet calculates with formulas such as =A1*B1; absolute references like $A$1 stay fixed when copied. Use spreadsheets for quick tables and programs for repeated work. Check units and significant figures.

sections.heading: Root finding
sections.text:
A root is x where f(x) = 0. Bisection needs a and b with f(a) and f(b) of opposite sign; it halves the interval and keeps the sign change. Newton-Raphson uses x_new = x − f(x) ÷ f′(x); it is faster but fails if f′ is zero.

Example: f(x) = x² − 2. With a = 1 (f = −1) and b = 2 (f = 2), midpoint 1.5 gives f = 0.25, so the root is in [1, 1.5]. True root is √2 ≈ 1.41421.

sections.heading: Interpolation and fitting
sections.text:
Interpolation estimates between known points. Linear interpolation between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) gives y = y1 + (x − x1)(y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1). Example: (1, 10) and (3, 20) give y at x = 2 as 10 + (1)(10) ÷ 2 = 15.

Curve fitting finds a formula for scattered data. A least-squares line y = a + bx has b = Σ((x − x̄)(y − ȳ)) ÷ Σ((x − x̄)²) and a = ȳ − b x̄. R² shows the fit; it does not prove cause.

sections.heading: Numerical integration
sections.text:
Numerical integration estimates area under a curve. The trapezoidal rule with step h uses h ÷ 2 × [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2fn−1 + fn]. Simpson’s rule, for an even number of intervals, uses h ÷ 3 × [f0 + 4f1 + 2f2 + ... + 4fn−1 + fn].

Example: integrate f(x) = x² from 0 to 2 with h = 1. Trapezoidal: 1 ÷ 2 × [0 + 2(1) + 4] = 3. Simpson: 1 ÷ 3 × [0 + 4(1) + 4] = 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.6667. Exact value is 8 ÷ 3.

keyPoints: An algorithm is a finite list of steps; variables store values, loops repeat steps and functions group reusable code.
Bisection halves a sign-change interval; Newton-Raphson uses x_new = x − f(x) ÷ f′(x).
Linear interpolation: y = y1 + (x − x1)(y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1).
A least-squares line y = a + bx has b = Σ((x − x̄)(y − ȳ)) ÷ Σ((x − x̄)²) and a = ȳ − b x̄.
Trapezoidal rule: h ÷ 2 × [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2fn−1 + fn]; Simpson’s rule: h ÷ 3 × [f0 + 4f1 + 2f2 + ... + 4fn−1 + fn].
Always check units, significant figures and whether a numerical result is physically sensible.

en.title: Reservoir rock properties
en.short: Porosity, permeability, saturation, wettability, capillary pressure, relative permeability and rock compressibility.

sections.heading: Porosity and saturation
sections.text:
Porosity phi is the fraction of bulk volume that is pore space: phi = Vp ÷ Vb. Effective porosity counts connected pores. Saturation is the fraction of pore volume held by a phase, and Sw + So + Sg = 1.

Example: a plug has bulk volume 20.0 cm³ and grain volume 17.0 cm³. Then Vp = 3.0 cm³ and phi = 3.0 ÷ 20.0 = 0.15, or 15%. If water volume is 1.2 cm³, Sw = 1.2 ÷ 3.0 = 0.40, or 40%.

sections.heading: Permeability and averaging
sections.text:
Permeability k measures flow capacity through connected pores. Darcy’s law for linear flow is Q = kAΔP ÷ (μL). With Q in cm³/s, A in cm², μ in cP, ΔP in atm and L in cm, k is in darcy; 1 D = 1000 mD.

Example: Q = 0.5 cm³/s, A = 5 cm², μ = 1 cP, L = 10 cm, ΔP = 2 atm. Then k = QμL ÷ (AΔP) = 0.5 × 1 × 10 ÷ (5 × 2) = 0.5 D = 500 mD.

For layers, horizontal flow uses the thickness-weighted arithmetic mean, vertical flow uses the harmonic mean, and random heterogeneity often uses the geometric mean.

sections.heading: Capillary pressure and wettability
sections.text:
Wettability is the rock’s preference for water or oil. Capillary pressure is Pc = Pnw − Pw, the pressure difference across a curved interface; it depends on pore size, interfacial tension and wettability. Relative permeability kr is phase effective permeability divided by absolute permeability; it varies with saturation, wettability and saturation direction, so curves show hysteresis.

Rock compressibility cp = (1 ÷ Vp)(dVp ÷ dp) describes pore-volume change with pressure. Porosity is measured by helium porosimetry, saturation by Dean-Stark or retort, wettability by contact angle or Amott tests, permeability by core flow, capillary pressure by porous plate, centrifuge or mercury injection, relative permeability by core floods, and compressibility by pore-volume change tests. Average by flow direction, and check current laboratory standards.

keyPoints: Porosity phi = Vp ÷ Vb; saturation fractions sum to 1.
Darcy’s law Q = kAΔP ÷ (μL); 1 D = 1000 mD.
Horizontal average permeability is thickness-weighted arithmetic; vertical average is harmonic.
Capillary pressure Pc = Pnw − Pw; relative permeability depends on saturation and wettability.
Rock compressibility cp = (1 ÷ Vp)(dVp ÷ dp).
Measure porosity by helium porosimetry, saturation by Dean-Stark, permeability by core flow, and check current standards.

en.title: Reservoir fluid properties and phase behaviour
en.short: Oil, gas and water properties, gas laws, PVT data, phase envelopes and reservoir correlations.

sections.heading: Fluid properties and PVT data
sections.text: Reservoir fluids are mixtures of hydrocarbons and water. Oil properties include density, viscosity, compressibility, bubble point, solution gas-oil ratio Rs and formation volume factor Bo. Gas properties include specific gravity, compressibility factor z, viscosity and gas formation volume factor Bg. Water properties include salinity, viscosity, compressibility and dissolved gas. PVT laboratory tests such as flash, differential liberation, separator tests and constant composition expansion measure how these change with pressure and temperature. Use measured data where possible; correlations are estimates.

sections.heading: Gas laws and EOS
sections.text: An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT. A real gas obeys PV = znRT, where z is the compressibility factor; z = 1 for an ideal gas. Equations of state such as Peng-Robinson and Soave-Redlich-Kwong predict phase behaviour from composition. Example: 1 kmol of gas at 300 K and 10,000 kPa with z = 0.9. Take R = 8.314 kPa·m³/(kmol·K). V = znRT ÷ P = 0.9 × 1 × 8.314 × 300 ÷ 10,000 = 0.224 m³.

sections.heading: Phase envelope
sections.text: A phase envelope plots pressure against temperature for a mixture. The bubble-point curve and the dew-point curve meet at the critical point. Inside the envelope two phases coexist; outside it the fluid is single phase. At temperatures above the critical point but below the highest temperature of the envelope, retrograde condensation can occur: liquid forms as pressure falls. Composition changes the shape and position of the envelope.

sections.heading: FVF, viscosity and correlations
sections.text: Formation volume factor relates reservoir volume to surface volume: Bo = oil volume at reservoir conditions ÷ stock-tank oil volume, and Bg = gas volume at reservoir conditions ÷ gas volume at standard conditions. Rs is the gas dissolved in oil at reservoir conditions. Viscosity rises for heavier oil and falls as temperature rises or more gas dissolves. Correlations such as Standing, Vazquez-Beggs and Lee-Gonzalez-Eakin estimate properties when laboratory data are missing. They are empirical, so check their ranges and use measured PVT data when available.

keyPoints: Real gas law: PV = znRT, with z = 1 for an ideal gas.
Bo = reservoir oil volume ÷ stock-tank oil volume; Bg = reservoir gas volume ÷ standard-condition gas volume.
A phase envelope separates single-phase from two-phase regions; bubble and dew curves meet at the critical point.
Rs is the solution gas-oil ratio, the gas dissolved in oil at reservoir conditions.
Correlations estimate fluid properties, but measured PVT data are preferred.
Viscosity depends on composition, pressure, temperature and dissolved gas.

en.title: Drilling systems and operations
en.short: Rotary rig systems, bits, drill string, fluids, hydraulics, directional drilling and well sequence.

sections.heading: Rig systems
sections.text:
A rotary rig turns a bit at the bottom of the hole while circulating fluid. Its main systems are hoisting (drawworks, the hoist winch, mast, travelling block), rotating (top drive or rotary table), circulating (mud pumps, standpipe, pits, shale shakers), power, and well control (blowout preventer).

The mast supports the string; the travelling block raises and lowers it. The blowout preventer is a barrier; well control has its own topic.

sections.heading: Bits and string
sections.text:
The bit cuts rock by scraping, crushing or shearing. Roller-cone bits have rotating cones with teeth or inserts. Fixed-cutter bits, usually polycrystalline diamond compact (PDC), shear rock with hard cutters.

The drill string is drill pipe, drill collars, stabilisers and tools. Drill collars are heavy tubes that supply weight on bit. The string transmits torque and carries fluid, and can carry measurement-while-drilling (MWD) tools that send inclination and azimuth to surface.

sections.heading: Fluids and hydraulics
sections.text:
Drilling fluid, or mud, cools the bit, carries cuttings, stabilises the borehole and helps control formation pressure. Mud goes down the string, through bit nozzles, and up the annulus. Annular velocity is v = Q ÷ A, where Q is flow rate and A is annular area.

Example: Q = 20 L/s = 0.020 m³/s, hole diameter 0.200 m, pipe diameter 0.127 m.
A = π ÷ 4 × (0.200² − 0.127²) = 0.01875 m²
v = 0.020 ÷ 0.01875 = 1.07 m/s

Too low a velocity leaves cuttings; too high erodes the hole.

sections.heading: Directional and sequence
sections.text:
Directional drilling controls inclination (angle from vertical) and azimuth (compass direction). It is used for offshore clusters, targets under obstacles and horizontal wells. A mud motor or rotary steerable system steers the bottom-hole assembly, and MWD gives survey data.

A well is drilled in stages: prepare the site, drill surface hole, run and cement casing, then drill the next, smaller hole. Each section is cased before the next begins.

keyPoints: A rotary rig has hoisting, rotating, circulating, power and well control systems.
Roller-cone bits crush and scrape; fixed-cutter (PDC) bits shear rock.
The drill string is drill pipe, drill collars, stabilisers and tools; collars supply weight on bit.
Drilling fluid cools the bit, carries cuttings, stabilises the hole and helps control formation pressure.
Annular velocity is v = Q ÷ A; check units before calculating.
Directional drilling controls inclination and azimuth, and each hole section is cased before the next is drilled.

en.title: Well design, cementing and well control
en.short: Casing design loads, primary cementing, kick detection and blowout prevention in well control.

sections.heading: Primary well control
sections.text:
Primary well control balances formation pressure with mud hydrostatic pressure. P = 0.00981 × ρ × TVD, where P is kPa, ρ is kg/m³ and TVD is m. Mud weight must exceed pore pressure by a trip margin but stay below fracture pressure.

Example: at TVD 2500 m, pore pressure is 27 MPa. Required density = 27,000 ÷ (0.00981 × 2500) = 1101 kg/m³. Add 50 kg/m³: 1151 kg/m³, giving 28.2 MPa.

sections.heading: Casing design
sections.text:
Casing strings (conductor, surface, intermediate, production) are designed for burst, collapse and tension. Design factors are multipliers on the load; companies and regulators set them, so they vary by country. API and ISO standards exist, but national rules may add requirements.

Tension check: a 2000 m string of 50 kg/m casing weighs 2000 × 50 × 9.81 = 981 kN. With a design factor of 1.6, required capacity is 1.6 × 981 = 1570 kN.

sections.heading: Cementing operations
sections.text: Primary cementing pumps slurry down the casing and up the annulus, displacing mud. Two plugs separate slurry from mud. Set cement isolates zones, supports casing and protects steel. Additives control density, thickening time and fluid loss. A cement bond log checks the result. Poor cementing lets fluids channel between zones. Acceptance tests and rules differ by country; check the regulator.

sections.heading: Kicks and blowouts
sections.text: A kick is an influx of formation fluid when formation pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure. Signs include pit gain, flow with pumps off, pump pressure changes and gas-cut mud. The crew shuts in using the blowout preventer (BOP): annular and ram preventers, choke manifold and kill line. Primary control is the mud column; secondary control is the BOP. A well kill circulates the influx out by the driller’s or wait-and-weight method. BOP tests and drills are required in most countries, but details vary. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering and NUPRC upstream operations; check current rules.

keyPoints: Hydrostatic pressure: P = 0.00981 × ρ × TVD, with P in kPa, ρ in kg/m³ and TVD in m.
Primary well control uses mud hydrostatic pressure; secondary control uses the blowout preventer.
Casing is designed for burst, collapse and tension, with design factors set by company policy and the national regulator.
A kick shows as pit gain, flow with pumps off or gas-cut mud; shut the well in immediately.
Primary cementing isolates zones and supports casing; a cement bond log checks the result.
BOP testing, crew drills and well control rules vary by country; always check the current national regulator.

en.title: Formation evaluation and well logging
en.short: Wireline and LWD logs, lithology, porosity, water saturation, permeability, and core integration.

sections.heading: Logs and tools
sections.text: Formation evaluation uses measurements from boreholes to estimate rock and fluid properties. Wireline logs are run on a cable after drilling; logging while drilling (LWD) tools are part of the drill string and measure during drilling. Common measurements: gamma ray (natural radioactivity, high in clay), resistivity (opposition to electric current, low in saline water, high in hydrocarbons), bulk density, neutron (hydrogen index), sonic (travel time) and caliper (hole diameter). Each responds to different properties, so logs are interpreted together.

sections.heading: Lithology and porosity
sections.text: Gamma ray and neutron-density crossplots separate sandstone, limestone, dolomite and shale. Density porosity is φ_D = (ρ_ma − ρ_b) ÷ (ρ_ma − ρ_f), where ρ_ma is matrix density, ρ_b is logged bulk density and ρ_f is fluid density. Example: ρ_b = 2.30 g/cm³, ρ_ma = 2.65 g/cm³, ρ_f = 1.00 g/cm³. φ_D = (2.65 − 2.30) ÷ (2.65 − 1.00) = 0.35 ÷ 1.65 = 0.212, or 21.2%. Sonic and neutron logs give independent porosity estimates; differences reveal lithology or gas.

sections.heading: Water saturation and permeability
sections.text: Archie’s equation for clean formations is S_w = [(a R_w) ÷ (φ^m R_t)]^(1/n), where R_w is water resistivity, R_t is true formation resistivity, and a, m, n are empirical constants (often a = 1, m = 2, n = 2). Example: φ = 0.20, R_w = 0.10 Ω·m, R_t = 10 Ω·m. S_w² = (1 × 0.10) ÷ (0.20² × 10) = 0.10 ÷ 0.40 = 0.25, so S_w = 0.50, or 50%. Permeability is not measured directly by logs; empirical correlations (for example Timur or Coates) use porosity and irreducible water saturation, and must be calibrated to core.

sections.heading: Integration and uncertainty
sections.text: Logs are calibrated against core porosity and core-derived Archie parameters from special core analysis (SCAL). Capillary pressure data build saturation-height functions. Production logs and well tests show which zones flow, and pressure transient tests estimate permeability. Shaly sands need corrections to Archie. Always report uncertainty: log resolution, mud filtrate invasion and bad hole affect results.

keyPoints: Wireline logs are run after drilling; LWD tools measure during drilling.
Density porosity: φ_D = (ρ_ma − ρ_b) ÷ (ρ_ma − ρ_f).
Archie’s equation: S_w = [(a R_w) ÷ (φ^m R_t)]^(1/n).
For a = 1, m = 2, n = 2: S_w = √(R_w ÷ (φ² R_t)).
Permeability from logs is empirical and must be calibrated to core.
Integrate logs with core, capillary pressure and production data, and state uncertainty.

en.title: Well completion and stimulation
en.short: Completion types, perforation, sand control, packers, tubing, acidising and basic hydraulic fracturing.

sections.heading: Completion choice
sections.text: A completion is the final interface between reservoir and wellbore. It controls how fluids enter and how zones are isolated. Main types are open hole, cased and perforated, liner or screen, and gravel packed. Open hole is cheap but gives little zonal isolation. Cased and perforated gives control and allows selective work. Screens and gravel packs suit unconsolidated sand. Selection depends on rock strength, pressure, fluid, zones, intervention needs and cost. Codes vary by country; check local rules.

sections.heading: Perforation, sand and packers
sections.text: Perforation uses shaped charges to make tunnels through casing, cement and rock. Shot density, phasing and underbalance affect productivity. Sand control stops formation sand from entering the well; options include screens, gravel packs, frac packs and chemical consolidation. Packers are elastomer seals that isolate the annulus between tubing and casing or liner, so zones can be produced or treated separately. A packer must hold pressure and survive temperature and chemicals.

sections.heading: Tubing and stimulation
sections.text:
Tubing is the inner pipe that carries produced fluids. Its diameter must pass the expected flow without excessive friction, and its material must resist pressure, corrosion and temperature. Acidising dissolves near-wellbore damage: hydrochloric acid for carbonates, and mud acid (hydrochloric plus hydrofluoric) for sandstone, always with inhibitors. Hydraulic fracturing pumps fluid above fracture pressure to create a crack, then carries proppant into it to keep it open. Acid fracturing etches carbonate faces.

Example: fracture 100 m long per wing, 20 m high, 0.005 m wide: 100 × 20 × 0.005 = 10 m³ per wing, 20 m³ for two wings before leak-off.

sections.heading: Matching reservoir
sections.text: Consolidated, permeable sandstone often suits cased and perforated. Weak, unconsolidated sand needs screens or gravel pack. Carbonates may be open hole or perforated and acidised. Tight, low-permeability rock is a candidate for hydraulic fracturing. Many zones favour packers or intelligent completions with valves. High pressure and corrosive fluids push tubing and completion metallurgy toward corrosion-resistant alloys. The final choice balances productivity, sand risk, control, intervention and cost.

keyPoints: Completion choice depends on rock strength, sand risk, zones, pressure, fluid and cost.
Open hole is cheap but gives little zonal isolation; cased and perforated allows selective control.
Perforation connects wellbore to reservoir; shot density, phasing and underbalance affect inflow.
Sand control options include screens, gravel packs, frac packs and chemical consolidation.
Packers isolate annulus zones; tubing diameter and metallurgy must suit flow, pressure and corrosion.
Acidising dissolves near-wellbore damage; hydraulic fracturing creates a propped fracture. Fracture volume for one wing ≈ length × height × width.

en.title: Reservoir engineering fundamentals
en.short: Volumetric oil in place, material balance, drive mechanisms and recovery factor calculations.

sections.heading: Volumetric estimate
sections.text: Volumetric estimation gives original oil in place from rock and fluid data: N = A h φ (1 − Sw) ÷ Bo. N is stock-tank oil volume, A is area, h is net pay, φ is porosity, Sw is water saturation, and Bo is oil formation volume factor, reservoir volume divided by stock-tank volume. Use consistent units; in SI, A in m², h in m and N in m³. The result assumes uniform properties and is static, not a forecast.

sections.heading: Material balance
sections.text: Material balance is volume accounting. It equates initial fluids to fluids remaining plus produced, allowing for gas cap expansion, water influx and injection. It checks the volumetric estimate. For an undersaturated oil reservoir (pressure above bubble point, so no free gas) with no gas cap, water influx or injection, and neglecting rock and water expansion, N = Np Bo ÷ (Bo − Boi), where Np is cumulative production and Boi is initial Bo. Small changes in Bo make this sensitive.

sections.heading: Drive mechanisms
sections.text: Drive mechanisms are energy sources that move hydrocarbons to wells. Solution gas drive uses gas released from oil as pressure falls. Gas cap expansion uses compressed gas above the oil. Water drive uses water from an aquifer. Gravity drainage separates fluids by density. Rock and water expansion and compaction also contribute. Pressure and production data help identify the drive.

sections.heading: Recovery factor
sections.text: Recovery factor RF is recoverable volume divided by original volume in place, so recoverable oil = N × RF. Example: A = 1,000,000 m², h = 20 m, φ = 0.20, Sw = 0.25, Bo = 1.25. N = 1,000,000 × 20 × 0.20 × (1 − 0.25) ÷ 1.25 = 2,400,000 m³. If RF = 0.30, recoverable oil = 2,400,000 × 0.30 = 720,000 m³. Recovery factors vary with rock, fluid and drive; use field data or official reserves definitions, which differ by country.

keyPoints: Volumetric oil in place: N = A h φ (1 − Sw) ÷ Bo, with consistent units.
Material balance is volume accounting and checks the volumetric estimate.
Simplified undersaturated oil tank model: N = Np Bo ÷ (Bo − Boi).
Main drive mechanisms are solution gas, gas cap, water drive, gravity drainage and compaction.
Recovery factor RF = recoverable volume ÷ original volume in place.
Recoverable oil = N × RF; recovery factors vary with rock, fluid and drive, so use field data.

en.title: Reservoir performance prediction and decline analysis
en.short: Decline curves, water influx, pressure transients and simulation for forecasting.

sections.heading: Decline curves
sections.text:
Decline curve analysis fits a trend to production and extrapolates it. The exponential model is q = qi e^(−Dt), where q is rate, qi is initial rate, t is time and D is nominal decline rate. Cumulative production is Np = (qi − q) ÷ D, with D and the rates in the same time units. When decline slows, the hyperbolic model q = qi (1 + b Di t)^(−1/b) fits better, where Di is initial decline rate; b = 0 is the exponential limit and b = 1 is harmonic decline.

Example: qi = 1,000 bbl/day and D = 0.01 per day. After 12 days, q = 1,000 × e^(−0.12) = 886.9 bbl/day. Np = (1,000 − 886.9) ÷ 0.01 = 11,310 bbl.

sections.heading: Water influx
sections.text: An aquifer can support a reservoir by pushing water into it. Water influx models estimate the volume, We, from pressure history. The Schilthuis steady-state model makes the influx rate proportional to the pressure drop. Van Everdingen-Hurst uses dimensionless time functions and superposition for changing pressure. Fetkovich applies material balance to a finite aquifer. We enters the reservoir material balance, so it affects reserves and pressure prediction.

sections.heading: Pressure transients
sections.text: Pressure transient tests record bottomhole pressure after a rate change. A drawdown test holds rate constant and measures falling pressure; a buildup test shuts the well in and measures recovery. In radial flow, pressure against log time is a straight line. Its slope gives permeability-thickness, kh; its position gives skin, S, a measure of near-well damage or stimulation. Later changes show faults, boundaries or interference.

sections.heading: Forecasting and simulation
sections.text: Production forecasting combines decline curves, water influx, material balance and well-test results. A forecast should state assumptions and give a range, not one number. Reservoir simulation is a numerical prediction tool. It divides the reservoir into grid cells and solves mass conservation and Darcy flow with fluid properties. Engineers history match past pressure and production, then forecast wells, aquifers and recovery schemes. Simulation needs good data; it does not replace judgement.

keyPoints: Exponential decline: q = qi e^(−Dt) and Np = (qi − q) ÷ D, with D and the rates in the same time units.
Hyperbolic decline: q = qi (1 + b Di t)^(−1/b); b = 0 is the exponential limit and b = 1 is harmonic.
Water influx models such as Schilthuis, van Everdingen-Hurst and Fetkovich estimate We from pressure history for the material balance.
In radial flow, a semilog plot of pressure against log time gives kh from the slope and skin from its position.
A production forecast should give a range and state its assumptions; decline extrapolation is uncertain.
Reservoir simulation solves grid-based mass conservation and Darcy flow, and needs history matching before prediction.

en.title: Production engineering and nodal analysis
en.short: Inflow and outflow performance, tubing and choke behaviour, nodal analysis and well optimisation.

sections.heading: Inflow performance
sections.text: Inflow performance describes how fast the reservoir delivers fluid at a given bottom-hole flowing pressure (Pwf). Drawdown is reservoir pressure Pr minus Pwf. For single-phase liquid flow, the productivity index J = q ÷ (Pr − Pwf), so q = J(Pr − Pwf). For two-phase oil flow, Vogel’s empirical equation is q ÷ qmax = 1 − 0.2(Pwf ÷ Pr) − 0.8(Pwf ÷ Pr)², where qmax is the rate at Pwf = 0. Gas wells often use q = C(Pr² − Pwf²)ⁿ. These are models.

sections.heading: Outflow and choke
sections.text: Outflow performance, or vertical lift performance (VLP), is the pressure needed at the tubing bottom to lift rate q to the wellhead. The pressure gradient has three parts: hydrostatic head, friction and acceleration. Tubing size, fluid properties and gas-liquid ratio change the VLP curve. A choke restricts flow. In critical flow the rate depends on upstream pressure only; in subcritical flow it depends on both pressures. Choke sizing uses field correlations.

sections.heading: Nodal analysis
sections.text: Nodal analysis divides the well at a node, often bottom-hole or wellhead, and plots inflow and outflow pressures against rate. The intersection is the operating point: the rate and pressure at which the well produces. Example: Pr = 250 bar, J = 2 m³/day/bar, and simplified VLP Pwf = 50 + 0.5q (bar, q in m³/day). The inflow performance relationship (IPR) gives q = 2(250 − Pwf). Substituting: q = 500 − 2(50 + 0.5q) = 400 − q, so q = 200 m³/day and Pwf = 150 bar. Check: 2(250 − 150) = 200; 50 + 0.5 × 200 = 150. Real VLP uses multiphase correlations.

sections.heading: Deliverability and optimisation
sections.text: Well deliverability is the range of rates a well can sustain at acceptable drawdown. Absolute open flow (AOF), mainly used for gas wells, is a theoretical maximum rate at zero flowing pressure, not a safe target. Optimisation compares the IPR with each possible VLP: tubing size, choke setting and completion. The best case is near the highest rate that still respects reservoir, sand, gas and facility limits. Local rules vary, so check official guidance.

keyPoints: Productivity index for single-phase liquid: J = q ÷ (Pr − Pwf).
Vogel’s equation for two-phase oil inflow: q ÷ qmax = 1 − 0.2(Pwf ÷ Pr) − 0.8(Pwf ÷ Pr)².
Gas well backpressure equation: q = C(Pr² − Pwf²)ⁿ, where C and n are empirical.
Nodal analysis finds the operating point where the inflow pressure curve meets the outflow (VLP) curve.
The VLP pressure gradient combines hydrostatic head, friction and acceleration.
Choke and tubing choices shift the VLP curve; optimisation seeks a stable rate within reservoir and facility limits.

en.title: Artificial lift systems
en.short: Gas lift, ESP and sucker rod pumping: principles, selection and basic design checks.

sections.heading: Selection
sections.text:
Artificial lift adds energy to a well when reservoir pressure can no longer lift the fluids to surface at the wanted rate. Selection compares the inflow performance (how much the reservoir can deliver) with the lift method’s capacity. Key criteria are target rate, depth, deviation, fluid viscosity, gas-oil ratio, water cut, sand or wax, available power or gas, maintenance access, and capital and operating cost. No method is best everywhere.

Design codes and company standards vary by country, so check the current local code and the operator’s standard.

sections.heading: Gas lift
sections.text: Gas lift injects gas into the tubing through valves. The gas lightens the fluid column, so the same bottomhole pressure supports a taller column and more oil flows. Continuous gas lift suits high-rate wells; intermittent lift suits low-rate wells. Design checks include injection gas pressure and volume, valve depth and unloading sequence, tubing size, compressor capacity, and flow stability.

sections.heading: Pumps
sections.text:
A sucker rod pump uses a surface beam unit to move rods and a downhole plunger. Its theoretical displacement is Q = 0.1166 × d² × S × N, where d is plunger diameter in inches, S is stroke in inches, N is strokes per minute, and Q is barrels per day. Example: d = 2 in, S = 60 in, N = 10 spm gives Q = 0.1166 × 4 × 60 × 10 = 280 bbl/day. At 80% volumetric efficiency, about 224 bbl/day. Check rod load, torque and pump fillage.

An electric submersible pump (ESP) is a multistage centrifugal pump with a motor and cable. Check intake pressure, free gas, viscosity, temperature and motor load. Other methods include progressing cavity pumps for viscous or sandy oil, hydraulic pumps, plunger lift and jet pumps.

keyPoints: Artificial lift is chosen by comparing inflow performance with lift capacity and well conditions.
Gas lift reduces the tubing fluid gradient by injecting gas through valves.
Sucker rod pump displacement: Q = 0.1166 × d² × S × N in bbl/day for d and S in inches and N in spm.
ESP design checks include intake pressure, free gas, viscosity, temperature and motor load.
Volumetric efficiency reduces theoretical pump rate; check rod load and pump fillage.
Design codes and standards differ by country; use the current local and company documents.

en.title: Surface production facilities and pipeline transport
en.short: Separation, crude and water treatment, metering, storage, flow assurance and pipelines.

sections.heading: Separation
sections.text: The wellstream arrives as a mixture of gas, crude oil and water. A separator uses gravity and retention time to let the phases settle. Gas leaves at the top, oil and water at lower outlets. Internals such as baffles, weirs and mist extractors improve separation. Stage separation, with two or three separators at falling pressures, lets gas break out gradually and reduces oil shrinkage. Separator size depends on flow rate, pressure, temperature and fluid properties, not on one universal rule.

sections.heading: Oil and water treatment
sections.text: Crude oil often carries water, which holds salt, as an emulsion of tiny droplets. Demulsifiers, heat and electrostatic coalescers help droplets merge and settle, taking out the water and most of the salt. Desalting, washing with fresh water, removes the rest. The oil is then stabilised by removing light gas so its vapour pressure is safe for storage. Produced water treatment removes dispersed oil and solids by skimmers, hydrocyclones, flotation or filtration before reinjection or disposal. Limits and permits differ by country, so check the current regulator’s rules.

sections.heading: Metering and storage
sections.text: Metering measures volume or mass for allocation, sales or custody transfer, where ownership changes and the measurement sets the bill. Orifice, turbine, Coriolis and ultrasonic meters are common; each needs calibration and correct installation. Storage tanks hold crude before export or refining. Tanks need gauging, water draw-off, vapour control and secondary containment. Tank design and inspection follow national rules and company standards, which vary, so use the current official code.

sections.heading: Flow assurance and pipelines
sections.text: Flow assurance keeps fluids moving from wellhead to market. Wax, hydrates, asphaltenes and scale can block lines, while slugs cause surges. Insulation, heating, chemicals and pigging manage them. Pipelines may carry single-phase or multiphase fluids; pumps or compressors supply pressure. For single-phase flow, pressure drop is estimated by Darcy-Weisbach: Δp = f(L ÷ D)(ρv² ÷ 2). Multiphase lines need two-phase correlations instead. Example: f = 0.02, L = 10,000 m, D = 0.3 m, ρ = 850 kg/m³, v = 1.5 m/s. Δp = 0.02 × (10,000 ÷ 0.3) × (850 × 1.5² ÷ 2) = 637,500 Pa, about 638 kPa. Codes and limits vary by country.

keyPoints: Separators use gravity and retention time to split gas, oil and water; stage separation reduces oil shrinkage.
Crude oil treatment removes water and salt by demulsifiers, heat, coalescence and desalting, then stabilises the oil.
Produced water is cleaned by skimmers, hydrocyclones, flotation or filtration before reinjection or disposal.
Metering needs calibrated meters; storage needs gauging, vapour control and containment.
Flow assurance manages wax, hydrates, scale and slugs by insulation, heating, chemicals and pigging.
Pipeline pressure drop for single-phase flow: Δp = f(L ÷ D)(ρv² ÷ 2); multiphase lines need two-phase correlations; design codes differ by country, so check the official source.

en.title: Natural gas engineering: properties, wells, processing and storage
en.short: Gas properties, well deliverability, compression, dehydration, processing, pipeline flow and storage.

sections.heading: Gas properties
sections.text:
Natural gas is a mixture, mostly methane. Its specific gravity is the ratio of its molecular mass to that of air (about 28.97). The real gas law is PV = ZnRT, where Z is the compressibility factor: Z = 1 for an ideal gas and differs from 1 as pressure rises. Density is ρ = PM ÷ (ZRT). Gas viscosity is low and, at low pressure, rises with temperature. At high pressure, use pseudo-pressure, a transform that accounts for changing μZ.

Example: 10 m³ of methane at 5 MPa and 300 K, Z = 0.90. n = PV ÷ (ZRT) = (5000 × 10) ÷ (0.90 × 8.314 × 300) = 22.3 kmol. Mass = 22.3 × 16.04 = 357 kg, so density = 35.7 kg/m³.

sections.heading: Wells and compression
sections.text: Gas well deliverability links pressure to flow. For steady radial flow, gas rate qg is proportional to (pr² − pwf²) ÷ (μZ T ln(re/rw)); pr and pwf are reservoir and flowing bottomhole pressures. The exact constant depends on the unit system. A high drawdown gives more gas, but liquid loading and sand can limit it. Compression raises pressure for transport or sales. Reciprocating compressors suit high pressure ratios; centrifugal machines suit large flows. Intercooling between stages reduces power and temperature. Surge is unstable flow in centrifugal compressors.

sections.heading: Dehydration and processing
sections.text: Water vapour forms hydrates, ice-like solids, and causes corrosion, so dehydration lowers the water dew point. Glycol absorption is common; molecular sieves give drier gas. Gas processing removes H2S and CO2 by sweetening, often with amines, recovers natural gas liquids and condensate, and sends dry sales gas. Sulfur recovery may follow.

sections.heading: Pipeline flow and storage
sections.text: Pipeline pressure drop depends on flow rate, pipe diameter, length, friction and gas density. The general energy equation with a friction factor is the basis; empirical equations are common. Storage balances summer and winter demand. Depleted reservoirs and salt caverns store gas; cushion gas remains permanently, working gas is withdrawn. LNG storage is different.

keyPoints: Real gas law: PV = ZnRT, with Z the compressibility factor.
Gas density: ρ = PM ÷ (ZRT); gas specific gravity compares molecular mass with air.
Gas well inflow depends on (pr² − pwf²) ÷ (μZ T ln(re/rw)).
Multistage compression uses intercooling; centrifugal compressors can surge.
Dehydration prevents hydrates and corrosion; sweetening removes H2S and CO2.
Pipeline pressure drop rises with flow and length and falls with diameter; storage uses cushion and working gas.

en.title: Petroleum refining basics
en.short: Crude characterisation, distillation, cracking, reforming, product specifications and refinery issues.

sections.heading: Crude characterisation
sections.text: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with sulphur, nitrogen, oxygen and metals. Refiners characterise it by density (API gravity), sulphur content, distillation curve and pour point. API gravity compares density with water: API = 141.5 ÷ SG − 131.5, where SG is specific gravity at 60°F. High API means lighter crude. Sweet crude has low sulphur; sour crude has more. The true boiling point (TBP) curve shows how much material boils in each temperature range. These properties decide refinery configuration and product yield.

sections.heading: Distillation
sections.text:
Distillation separates crude by boiling range. Atmospheric distillation runs near atmospheric pressure and makes gases, naphtha, kerosene, diesel and atmospheric residue. Vacuum distillation distils the residue at low pressure so heavy gas oil can boil without thermal cracking. Fractionation uses trays or packing; lighter components rise and condense higher in the column.

Example: 20,000 b/d feed with 30% naphtha by volume gives 0.30 × 20,000 = 6,000 b/d naphtha. Actual cut points and yields vary with crude and operation.

sections.heading: Conversion processes
sections.text: Conversion processes change molecular size or shape. Cracking breaks large molecules into smaller ones: thermal cracking uses heat; catalytic cracking uses a catalyst, often fluid catalytic cracking (FCC); hydrocracking adds hydrogen. Reforming rearranges naphtha molecules into aromatics and branched molecules with higher octane number, producing hydrogen. Hydrotreating removes sulphur and nitrogen with hydrogen. Alkylation and isomerisation improve gasoline blending. These units let a refinery match crude to product demand.

sections.heading: Products and issues
sections.text:
Product specifications are limits on properties such as octane number (petrol anti-knock quality), cetane number (diesel ignition quality), vapour pressure, flash point, distillation range and sulphur. Environmental issues include sulphur dioxide, carbon dioxide, water use and waste; limits differ by country and change, so check current official rules. Economics depend on crude price, product prices, refinery complexity, energy use and utilisation.

A simple sulphur balance: if feed sulphur is 2.0% and hydrotreating removes 90%, product sulphur is 2.0 × (1 − 0.90) = 0.20% by mass.

keyPoints: API gravity = 141.5 ÷ SG − 131.5, with SG at 60°F.
Atmospheric distillation separates by boiling range; vacuum distillation recovers heavy gas oil without thermal cracking.
Cracking breaks large molecules; reforming rearranges naphtha to raise octane number and make hydrogen.
Product specifications cover octane or cetane number, vapour pressure, flash point, sulphur and distillation range.
Cut yield = feed rate × volume fraction.
Sulphur remaining = feed sulphur × (1 − removal fraction).

en.title: Enhanced oil recovery: methods, screening and design
en.short: Chemical, thermal, gas and microbial EOR, screening, displacement mechanisms and project design.

sections.heading: Displacement mechanisms
sections.text:
Enhanced oil recovery (EOR) is the injection of energy or fluids to recover oil left after primary and secondary production. Overall recovery is the product of two factors: E = E_D × E_V. E_D, displacement efficiency, is how well fluid sweeps oil from the pores it enters; E_V, volumetric (sweep) efficiency, is the fraction of the reservoir the injected fluid actually reaches.

Mobility ratio compares how easily the injected fluid moves to how easily the oil moves: M = (k_rw ÷ μ_w) ÷ (k_ro ÷ μ_o), using relative permeability k_r and viscosity μ. If M is greater than 1 the injected fluid fingers through the oil and sweep falls. Most EOR methods aim to lower M or to reduce the oil left behind in swept pores.

sections.heading: Chemical and gas methods
sections.text:
Chemical EOR adds polymer, surfactant or alkali to water. Polymer raises water viscosity, lowering M and improving sweep. Surfactant lowers interfacial tension between oil and water so trapped droplets can move. Alkali reacts with acidic crude to form surfactant in place. The three are often combined as alkali-surfactant-polymer (ASP) flooding.

Gas EOR injects carbon dioxide, hydrocarbon gas or nitrogen. If injected above a minimum miscibility pressure the gas mixes with oil and displaces it completely in swept zones; otherwise it works by swelling the oil and lowering its viscosity. Gas tends to rise and to finger, so water-alternating-gas (WAG) injection is common.

sections.heading: Thermal and microbial methods
sections.text:
Thermal EOR suits heavy, viscous oil. Steam flooding injects steam continuously; cyclic steam stimulation (huff and puff) injects, soaks, then produces from the same well. Heat lowers viscosity, expands the oil and distills light ends. In-situ combustion burns part of the oil to generate heat and drive oil forward.

Microbial EOR uses bacteria to produce gases, acids, surfactants or biomass that improve displacement or block thief zones. It is still largely at pilot stage, and results vary with reservoir conditions.

sections.heading: Screening and design
sections.text:
Screening compares a candidate reservoir with published criteria tables covering oil gravity, viscosity, depth, permeability, oil saturation and temperature. These tables are guides only, and the ranges differ between sources; check current published criteria and run laboratory and simulation work.

Design steps: define the target oil, test fluids in the laboratory, build a reservoir model, forecast incremental oil and cost, then plan pilot monitoring.

Example: if laboratory work gives E_D = 0.60 and simulation gives E_V = 0.70, then E = 0.60 × 0.70 = 0.42, so 42% of the oil in place is recovered (60% of the oil in the swept region). If recovery without EOR would be 30% of oil in place, the incremental oil is 42 − 30 = 12% of oil in place, and the project is judged on that increment against its cost.

keyPoints: Overall recovery E = E_D × E_V, displacement efficiency times sweep efficiency.
Mobility ratio M = (k_rw ÷ μ_w) ÷ (k_ro ÷ μ_o); values above 1 cause fingering and poor sweep.
Chemical EOR uses polymer for sweep, surfactant and alkali for displacement.
Gas EOR works by miscible displacement, oil swelling and viscosity reduction; WAG controls fingering.
Thermal EOR lowers viscosity of heavy oil by steam or in-situ combustion.
Screening tables are guides only; confirm with laboratory tests, simulation and a monitored pilot.

en.title: Petroleum economics and reserves evaluation
en.short: Cash flow, discounting, NPV, fiscal regimes, risk, and reserves classification.

sections.heading: Cash flow and NPV
sections.text:
Cash flow is money actually moving in or out of a project in each period. A future amount is worth less today, so we discount it: PV = C ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ, where r is the discount rate and n is the number of periods. Net present value is NPV = Σ Cₜ ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ − C₀. Accept a project if NPV is positive.

Example: C₀ = 100 million, C₁ = 40 million, C₂ = 50 million, C₃ = 60 million, r = 10%.
PV₁ = 40 ÷ 1.1 = 36.36
PV₂ = 50 ÷ 1.21 = 41.32
PV₃ = 60 ÷ 1.331 = 45.08
NPV = 36.36 + 41.32 + 45.08 − 100 = 22.76 million.

sections.heading: Fiscal regimes
sections.text: A fiscal regime is the set of rules a country uses to share petroleum value between company and state. In a concessionary system the company pays royalty and tax. In a production sharing contract it recovers costs through cost oil and shares profit oil with the state. In a service contract it is paid a fee. Royalty, tax, cost recovery limits and state shares differ by country and contract, so use current terms.

sections.heading: Risk and uncertainty
sections.text: Risk is a known chance of loss; uncertainty is when outcomes and probabilities are not known. Expected value weights outcomes by probability: EV = Σ pᵢ × Vᵢ. If a project has a 60% chance of NPV 30 million and a 40% chance of NPV −10 million, EV = 0.6 × 30 + 0.4 × (−10) = 14 million. Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time; Monte Carlo simulation samples many inputs together.

sections.heading: Reserves classification
sections.text: Reserves are commercially recoverable volumes. The SPE Petroleum Resources Management System (SPE-PRMS) is widely used: proved (1P), proved plus probable (2P), and proved plus probable plus possible (3P). Contingent resources are not yet commercial; prospective resources are undiscovered. The US SEC has its own rules for listed companies, and national regulators such as Nigeria’s NUPRC may use local definitions. Check the governing system before reporting volumes.

keyPoints: NPV = Σ Cₜ ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ − C₀; discount each cash flow to today.
PV = C ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ and the discount factor is 1 ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ.
Expected value is EV = Σ pᵢ × Vᵢ; it does not remove risk.
Fiscal regimes include concessionary, production sharing and service contracts; terms vary by country.
SPE-PRMS classes reserves as 1P, 2P and 3P; contingent and prospective resources are not reserves.
Regulatory definitions differ by country; check current national rules before booking volumes.

en.title: Health, safety and environment in petroleum operations
en.short: Hazards, risk assessment, process and personal safety, waste, spills and emergency response.

sections.heading: Hazards and risk
sections.text:
A hazard is a source of harm; risk is the chance and severity of that harm. Hazard identification uses checklists, HAZID (hazard identification) workshops and HAZOP (hazard and operability) studies of process deviations. Risk assessment combines likelihood and consequence, often on a matrix.

On an illustrative 1 to 5 scale, likelihood 3 and severity 4 give a score of 12. If the company action level is 10, the task needs controls before work starts. Scales and action levels vary by company and country, so use the site procedure.

sections.heading: Process and personal safety
sections.text:
Process safety protects against major accidents such as fires, explosions and toxic releases. It relies on barriers: containment, pressure relief, gas detection, emergency shutdown and management of change. A permit to work is a formal written control for hot work and confined-space entry.

Personal safety protects the individual through training, protective equipment and safe procedures. Upstream hazards include well pressure and hydrogen sulphide; downstream hazards include flammable vapours and hot surfaces.

sections.heading: Environment and waste
sections.text:
Environmental impacts include air emissions, flaring, produced water, drilling cuttings and soil or groundwater contamination. An environmental impact assessment identifies these before a project starts. Waste management follows a hierarchy: prevent, reuse, recycle, treat, then dispose.

Spill response means notifying the authorities, stopping the source, containing the spill, recovering product and disposing of waste. Rules differ by country, so check the current national regulator.

sections.heading: Emergency response
sections.text:
An emergency response plan sets roles, alarms, muster points, shutdown steps and communication. Drills test it. Upstream emergencies include blowouts and pipeline leaks; downstream emergencies include tank fires and toxic releases.

Response follows an incident command structure, with notification to authorities and, where available, mutual aid. After any incident, investigate to find root causes and correct them.

keyPoints: A hazard is a source of harm; risk combines likelihood and severity.
Hazard identification uses checklists, HAZID and HAZOP; risk assessment ranks findings and sets controls.
Process safety uses independent barriers such as containment, relief, detection and shutdown.
Personal safety depends on training, protective equipment and permit-controlled work.
Waste management follows prevent, reuse, recycle, treat, dispose; spills need prompt notification, source control, containment and recovery.
Emergency plans define roles, alarms, muster and shutdown, and must be practised and reviewed.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and engineering regulation
en.short: Ethics, professional codes, API and ISO standards, and registration such as COREN.

sections.heading: Ethics and conduct
sections.text:
Professional ethics are principles for resolving conflicts between duties to employers, clients, colleagues and the public. A code of conduct turns them into rules: work within your competence, keep accurate records, protect confidentiality, declare conflicts of interest, avoid bribery, and put public safety, health and environment first. A conflict of interest exists when personal benefit could improperly influence judgement.

Case: Ngozi, a junior drilling engineer in Port Harcourt, is asked to sign a pressure-test record she did not see. She should refuse, tell her supervisor in writing, and report through approved channels. Codes differ, but truthfulness and public protection are common duties.

sections.heading: Codes and standards
sections.text:
Design codes and standards are agreed technical rules for design, materials, testing and operation. API standards are published by the American Petroleum Institute and widely used in oil and gas. ISO standards are published by the International Organization for Standardization. A standard is not law unless a regulation, contract or company procedure requires it. Use the edition named in the project basis and check amendments.

Codes give minimum requirements and do not replace engineering judgement. Where local regulation is stricter, it applies. Record the code and edition used for safety and liability.

sections.heading: Registration and regulation
sections.text:
Registration is legal recognition by a competent authority. In Nigeria, COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria, is the statutory regulator. It registers engineers and regulates practice; the Nigerian Society of Engineers (NSE) is a professional society, not the regulator. Requirements commonly include an accredited qualification, supervised experience and a professional assessment, but they change, so check COREN’s rules.

Other countries have their own bodies and laws, such as the Engineering Council in the United Kingdom and state licensing boards in the United States. Protected titles and permitted work vary. Confirm what your role and country require before signing or approving engineering work.

keyPoints: A conflict of interest exists when personal benefit could improperly influence professional judgement.
Codes of conduct require competence, honesty, confidentiality and priority for public safety, health and environment.
API and ISO standards are technical standards; they bind only when adopted by law, contract or company procedure.
In Nigeria, COREN is the statutory engineering regulator, while the Nigerian Society of Engineers is a professional society.
Registration requirements and protected titles differ by country, so check current official rules before signing engineering work.
Use the edition of a code named in the project basis and record it.

en.title: Research methods and the petroleum engineering design project
en.short: Literature review, problem framing, data methods, analysis, reporting and project planning.

sections.heading: Question and review
sections.text:
Research begins with a question, not a topic. Problem formulation turns a broad interest into a clear, answerable question: what will be measured, under what conditions, and what would count as a useful answer? State objectives, scope, assumptions and constraints.

A literature review is a structured search and critical summary of existing work, not a list of papers. Use journals, conference papers, standards and reputable reports; record search terms and selection rules. The review should show what is known, where methods disagree, and the gap your project addresses.

sections.heading: Data and methods
sections.text:
Data collection may use primary data you gather or secondary data already recorded. Define sampling, units, instruments, calibration and error sources before collection. Experimental methods use controlled tests, repeated runs and uncertainty analysis. Field-data methods use measurements such as production records, pressure surveys or logs; such data are often incomplete, noisy or confidential, so seek permission, check quality and document gaps.

A small case: Amina studies gas flaring at a Niger Delta field. She reviews public and operator reports, uses measured flare volumes and operating logs, checks units, and reports missing periods rather than filling them silently.

sections.heading: Analysis and report
sections.text:
Analysis turns data into evidence. Use descriptive statistics, plots, uncertainty ranges and sensitivity checks; compare results with theory or published values. Do not confuse correlation with cause.

A technical report usually has abstract, introduction, aims, methods, results, discussion, conclusions, references and appendices. Write so another student could repeat the work: give units, assumptions, data sources and limitations. Cite sources honestly and avoid plagiarism.

sections.heading: Planning and design
sections.text:
Plan the project with a timeline, milestones, supervisor meetings, a risk list and a data-management plan. For a design project, define the duty, constraints and success criteria, then compare options.

Identify the codes and standards that apply where the facility will be built; they differ by country, and professional registration rules do too (COREN in Nigeria, for example). Check official sources. Leave time for review, revision and a final check of calculations.

keyPoints: A research project starts with a focused, answerable question and clear objectives, scope and constraints.
A literature review is a critical, documented search that identifies the gap your project addresses.
Define sampling, units, calibration and error sources before collecting experimental or field data.
Analyse data with uncertainty and sensitivity checks, and do not treat correlation as proof of cause.
Write reports so another student can repeat the work, with units, assumptions, sources and limitations.
Plan with milestones and risk checks, and use the codes and registration rules of the country where the facility will be built (for example COREN in Nigeria).

en.title: Advanced reservoir simulation
en.short: Discretisation, grids, stability, upscaling, history matching, uncertainty and forecasting.

sections.heading: Discretising the equations
sections.text:
Reservoir flow follows mass conservation and Darcy’s law. For phase p: ∂(φ ρp Sp)/∂t + ∇·(ρp up) = qp, with up = −(k krp/μp)(∇p − ρp g ∇z). Here φ is porosity, S saturation, ρ density, u Darcy velocity, k permeability, kr relative permeability, μ viscosity and q source or sink.

A finite-volume method integrates this equation over each grid cell. Face fluxes are pressure differences times transmissibility, giving algebraic equations. Relative permeability, viscosity and density depend on pressure and saturation, so the equations are nonlinear and solved by Newton iteration.

sections.heading: Grids, steps and stability
sections.text:
Grids must resolve important geology and flow paths. Fine grids improve accuracy but cost more. Time steps control error and stability.

For explicit saturation transport, the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition limits the step. In one dimension, Δt ≤ φ Δx ÷ |u|, where u is the Darcy flux.

Example: φ = 0.20, Δx = 10 m, u = 0.04 m/day.
Δt ≤ 0.20 × 10 ÷ 0.04 = 50 days.

Implicit methods allow larger steps but need more work per step and can add numerical diffusion.
