sections.heading: Upscaling and history matching
sections.text:
Upscaling replaces a fine geological grid with a coarser simulation grid. Static upscaling averages properties such as porosity; dynamic upscaling tries to preserve flow behaviour. Upscaled relative permeability may differ from fine-grid curves.

History matching adjusts uncertain parameters, such as permeability or fault transmissibility, so the model reproduces observed pressures and production. The problem is non-unique: many parameter sets fit the data. Engineers use assisted methods and keep geological realism.

sections.heading: Uncertainty and forecasting
sections.text:
Uncertainty comes from geology, fluid properties, operations and model error. Monte Carlo simulation samples uncertain inputs and runs many models. Bayesian methods update prior distributions with production data. Ensembles of history-matched models represent uncertainty better than one fit.

Forecasts should report a range, not a single number. Summaries are P10, P50, P90, where P90 is the value that has a 90 per cent chance of being exceeded. Forecasts are conditional on assumptions and should be updated with new data.

keyPoints: Reservoir simulation solves mass conservation with Darcy’s law on a grid, usually by finite volumes.
The phase equations are nonlinear because relative permeability, viscosity and density depend on pressure and saturation; Newton iteration is common.
For explicit saturation transport, the one-dimensional CFL limit is Δt ≤ φ Δx ÷ |u|, where u is the Darcy flux.
Implicit time stepping allows larger steps but costs more per step and can add numerical diffusion.
Upscaling must preserve flow behaviour, not only average porosity.
History matching is non-unique, so uncertainty should be carried into forecasts as a range such as P10, P50 and P90.

en.title: Petroleum geomechanics
en.short: In-situ stress, pore pressure, failure, wellbore stability, sand, fractures and subsidence.

sections.heading: Stress and pore pressure
sections.text: In-situ stress is the stress in the ground before drilling. Vertical stress is overburden weight: σv = ∫ρg dz, about 23 kPa per metre. Horizontal stresses come from tectonics and compaction; leak-off tests and minifracs measure them. Pore pressure Pp is the fluid pressure in the pores. Effective stress is σ' = σ − αPp (Terzaghi with α = 1, or Biot, where α is the Biot coefficient). Rock fails on effective stress. Normal faulting needs σv > σH > σh; reverse faulting needs σH > σh > σv.

sections.heading: Failure and wellbore stability
sections.text: Mohr-Coulomb failure is τ = c + σn' tanφ, or σ1' = UCS + q σ3', where q = (1 + sinφ) ÷ (1 − sinφ) and UCS = 2c cosφ ÷ (1 − sinφ). Tensile failure occurs at σ3' = −T0, the tensile strength. The Kirsch solution gives the hoop stress around a circular wellbore. High hoop stress causes breakouts; low hoop stress causes tensile fractures. The safe mud weight lies between the pore pressure gradient and the fracture gradient. Deviated wells and depleted zones narrow this window.

sections.heading: Sand, fractures, subsidence
sections.text: Sand production follows shear failure of weak rock or perforation tunnels when drawdown is too high. Controls include limiting drawdown, screens and gravel packs. Hydraulic fractures open against the minimum stress σh. Linear elastic fracture mechanics uses the stress intensity factor KI; the fracture grows when KI ≥ KIc, the toughness. Width and length depend on fluid volume, leak-off and elasticity (PKN and KGD models). Depletion raises effective stress and compacts the reservoir. At the surface this is subsidence; the Ekofisk field in Norway is a well-known case.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
At 2,000 m with ρ = 2,300 kg/m³:
σv = 2,300 × 9.81 × 2,000 = 45.1 MPa
With Pp = 19.6 MPa and α = 1, σv' = 25.5 MPa.
If σh' = 10 MPa, c = 5 MPa and φ = 30°:
UCS = 2 × 5 × cos30° ÷ (1 − sin30°) = 17.3 MPa
q = (1 + sin30°) ÷ (1 − sin30°) = 3
Strength = 17.3 + 3 × 10 = 47.3 MPa, above 25.5 MPa, so stable.

keyPoints: Effective stress σ' = σ − αPp controls rock deformation and failure, where α is the Biot coefficient.
Vertical stress is the overburden weight, σv = ∫ρg dz; horizontal stresses are measured by leak-off tests and minifracs.
Mohr-Coulomb: σ1' = UCS + q σ3', with q = (1 + sinφ) ÷ (1 − sinφ) and UCS = 2c cosφ ÷ (1 − sinφ).
The mud weight window lies between pore pressure and fracture gradient, bounded by breakouts and tensile fractures.
A hydraulic fracture opens against σh and grows when KI ≥ KIc; PKN and KGD models estimate width and length.
Depletion raises effective stress, causing compaction, sand production and surface subsidence.

en.title: Unconventional resources and advanced hydraulic fracturing
en.short: Shale, tight gas and heavy oil, horizontal wells, multistage fracturing, resource assessment and regulation.

sections.heading: Resource types
sections.text:
Unconventional resources are hydrocarbons in rock too tight or too viscous for ordinary vertical wells to drain economically.

Shale is fine-grained, organic-rich rock; its oil or gas sits in tiny pores and partly adsorbed on organic matter. Tight gas lies in low-permeability sandstone or carbonate. Heavy oil is petroleum with high viscosity and low API gravity; exact cut-offs vary.

sections.heading: Drilling and fracturing
sections.text:
Horizontal drilling steers a well from vertical to a lateral that follows the target layer, increasing reservoir contact. Multistage hydraulic fracturing divides the lateral into stages.

Plugs or packers isolate a stage, perforations connect the well to rock, and pumps inject fluid faster than the rock accepts it. Pressure rises until fractures open. Proppant, usually sand or ceramic grains, keeps fractures partly open. The stimulated volume is large, but fracture geometry is uncertain and is monitored by microseismic and pressure data.

sections.heading: Resource assessment
sections.text:
Resource assessment estimates hydrocarbon in place and how much can be recovered. A play is a region with similar geology. Volumetric estimates use area, net thickness, porosity, saturation and formation volume factor. Technically recoverable volume is in-place volume times a recovery factor. Probabilistic methods report P90, P50 and P10 ranges, not one number.

Example: area = 100 km², net thickness = 30 m, porosity = 0.06, gas saturation = 0.7, gas formation volume factor = 0.005 reservoir m³ per standard m³.
In-place gas = 100×10⁶ × 30 × 0.06 × 0.7 ÷ 0.005 = 25.2×10⁹ standard m³.
At recovery factor 0.2, recoverable gas = 5.04×10⁹ standard m³.

sections.heading: Environment and regulation
sections.text:
Hydraulic fracturing raises water use, groundwater protection, produced water, methane emissions, land disturbance and induced seismicity concerns.

Rules differ by country and often by state or province. In Nigeria, upstream operations are regulated by the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, with environmental oversight under national environment law. In the United States, state oil and gas commissions regulate operational details, while federal rules cover some air and water issues. Check national and local rules.

keyPoints: Unconventional resources include shale oil and gas, tight gas and heavy oil, each defined by low permeability or high viscosity rather than one global cut-off.
Horizontal wells increase contact with the target layer, and multistage fracturing creates many connected fracture stages along the lateral.
In-place gas volume can be estimated as A × h × φ × Sg ÷ Bg, where Bg is the gas formation volume factor.
Technically recoverable volume equals in-place volume times a recovery factor, and probabilistic methods report P90, P50 and P10 ranges.
Hydraulic fracturing raises water, groundwater, methane, land and induced seismicity concerns, and rules differ by country and often by state or province.
In Nigeria the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission regulates upstream operations; in the United States state commissions and federal rules share roles, so check current rules.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in petroleum engineering
en.short: Designing, conducting and defending a master’s dissertation in petroleum engineering.

sections.heading: Research design
sections.text: A master’s dissertation answers one focused question with evidence. Begin with a research design: the plan linking question, theory, data and analysis. The question must be answerable within your time and access to wells, fields or company records. State aims and hypotheses. Choose a strategy such as experiment, simulation study, survey, case study or mixed methods. Mixed methods combine numbers and meanings, but only when each part serves the question.

sections.heading: Literature and methods
sections.text: Literature synthesis groups prior work by theme, compares methods and findings, and identifies the gap you address. Use a reproducible search: databases, terms, inclusion rules and dates. Quantitative methods measure variables and test relationships. Qualitative methods explore meanings, practices and context through interviews, documents or observation. Sampling must fit the aim: random sampling supports statistical generalisation; purposive sampling selects information-rich cases. Explain validity (measuring what you claim) and reliability (consistent repeated measurement).

sections.heading: Data and ethics
sections.text: Data quality covers accuracy, completeness, consistency and traceability. Keep a data management plan: file names, backups, version control and access rules. Calibrate instruments and record units. Pilot interview guides and transcribe carefully. Ethics approval is normally required before collecting data from people. Confidential company records also need the owner’s written permission. Obtain informed consent, protect anonymity and store data securely. Rules vary by country and institution, so check your university’s current policy. Example: a student in Port Harcourt, Nigeria studying gas flare effects needs residents’ consent, anonymised household data and committee approval.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: Write the thesis as an argument, not a diary. Typical chapters are introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion and conclusion; exact requirements vary by university. Each chapter should answer why it is there. Report limitations honestly. In the defence, summarise the question, method, main finding and contribution in a few minutes. Expect questions on sampling, data quality and alternative explanations. Reread your methods and results beforehand. A defence is a scholarly conversation, not an attack.

keyPoints: A dissertation is built around one focused, feasible research question.
Research design links question, theory, data and analysis; mixed methods need a clear purpose.
Literature synthesis compares and groups prior work to identify the gap, not list papers.
Quantitative methods test relationships; qualitative methods explore meaning and context; sampling must match the aim.
Data quality means accuracy, completeness, consistency and traceability; ethics approval and informed consent are normally required.
The defence tests your understanding of method, data quality and limitations, so prepare a short clear summary.
